Morose

/muh-ROHS/ - rhymes with dose · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Morose means sunk in gloom that has settled in and pushes company away.

After the bakery turned down his sourdough, Amos was morose for a week, kneading in silence and glaring at the proofing loaves.

Worked Example

Nobody could tease the old ferryman out of his morose spells: whole crossings passed in sighs and one-word answers, the passengers' jokes sinking into the grey water behind the boat.

Morose is deeper than a bad mood: settled gloom with a sullen, unsociable edge. A glum person is quiet for an afternoon; a morose one has let the darkness move in and answer the door.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

sullen: Sullen is silent resentment: the slammed door, the one-word answers aimed at whoever caused the mood. Morose shares the gloom but drops the grudge — a morose person is sunk in darkness that has settled in for weeks, not punishing anyone in particular.

melancholy: Melancholy means gently, thoughtfully sad — wistful autumn evenings, old letters, a mood a person can almost enjoy. Morose strips away that sweetness: the gloom turns heavy and unsociable, with a sullen edge that pushes company away rather than inviting quiet reflection.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

jovial: heartily, laughingly good-humored

chipper: briskly cheerful and energetic

Where it sits · how deeply the low spirits settle in — glum → morose → despairing

glum vs. morose: Glum is milder than morose — a passing afternoon of low spirits, while morose is gloom that settles in and turns sullen.

despairing vs. morose: Despairing goes further than morose — beyond gloom into the conviction that nothing will ever improve.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mor

Root — mor: mood, habit (Latin mos, moris)

Suffix — -ose

Suffix — -ose: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Mor (mood, habit) + -ose (full of) = full of one's own moods. Latin morosus described someone shut inside their own temperament, and that is still the picture: a morose person is barricaded in with their gloom, answering the world in sighs.

Use the root in a new word: morale

Use the root in a new word: morale: One daring rescue at sea lifted the whole fleet's morale for a month.

Word Choice

neutral to literary

Morose is settled gloom with a sullen edge — days or weeks of it, not a passing cloud. 'Glum' covers an afternoon; morose moves in and unpacks. And where its unit-mate dour describes only the stern, unsmiling surface, morose reports the weather inside: genuinely dark. A dour face can hide contentment; a morose one never does.
